# MULA — Calm Plant & Flower Care App for iPhone (soil-check watering reminders)

> MULA (App Store name “MULA: Plant Care”) is a calm, paper-textured plant and flower care app for iPhone (iOS 17+) and iPad (iPadOS 17+), also on Apple silicon Macs, with an Apple Watch app (watchOS 10+), Home and Lock Screen widgets and Siri, made by independent developer Gül Eda Aydemir. Instead of telling you to water on a fixed day, it asks how the soil feels (“Dry” logs a watering, “A little moist” asks again in 2 days, “Wet” skips the round). Every plant has a four-season care plan (water and feeding intervals, feeding pauses in the resting season, Southern hemisphere switch). It knows 20 plants (monstera, camellia, rubber plant, hydrangea, moth orchid, Chinese money plant, snake plant, peace lily, pothos, lavender, aloe, rose, tulip, cactus, Boston fern, English ivy, begonia, poinsettia, rosemary, areca palm) and any other plant with a general plan. Also: Emergency Care for very late checks, on-device photo identification of plant kinds, a photo journal with cut-paper plant portraits and posters, calm reminder sounds and garden music, Light Paper and Dark Forest themes. MULA Premium (Annual with a 1-week free trial, or Lifetime) adds unlimited plants (free: 10), plan editing, Vacation mode with a care sheet for plant sitters, a camera light meter (lux estimate), frost and heat alerts from Apple Weather for balcony plants, and answer buttons on larger widgets and Apple Watch. No ads, no account, no tracking; the garden stays on the iPhone and in the user's own iCloud (backup, sync across devices, optional shared garden), with only anonymous usage statistics sent (Google Analytics for Firebase, can be turned off). App interface in English; website in English, Turkish and Spanish.

# MULA quick-start guide: add your first plants, answer soil checks and set gentle reminders
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/mula-quick-start-guide/
Language: en

**Short answer:** To start with MULA, add a plant with a nickname, an optional species (or the “General care plan”), where it lives and how much light it gets, then allow notifications. When a plant’s interval is up, MULA asks how the soil feels instead of ordering a watering, and it only logs one when you answer “Dry”. The basics are free for up to 10 plants; MULA Premium adds unlimited plants and extras such as plan editing, the light meter and Vacation mode.

- Add a plant with a nickname, an optional species, where it lives (Indoor, Balcony or Outdoor) and its light.
- MULA asks “How does Momo’s soil feel?” and logs a watering only when you answer “Dry”.
- Three tabs: Today for what needs you, Garden for your plants, Settings for reminders and the look of the app.
- Pick a reminder time and quiet hours; reminders never come at night or more than once a day per plant.
- Free keeps up to 10 plants and 5 photos each; Premium is Annual (with a 1-week free trial) or Lifetime.

## How do I start using MULA?

MULA is a calm plant and flower care app for iPhone (iOS 17 or later) and iPad, which also runs on Macs with Apple silicon, with an Apple Watch app, widgets and Siri. Getting started takes a few minutes: add a plant, tell MULA where it lives and how much light it gets, and allow a gentle reminder. There is no account to create, and your garden is stored on your iPhone, not on a server.

On first launch, after a short welcome (“Every plant has its rhythm.”), MULA asks “Would you like a gentle reminder?”. That is the iPhone’s notification permission. Then you tap “Begin my garden”. The app’s interface is in English.

- [ ] Add your first plant
- [ ] Choose where it lives and how much light it gets
- [ ] Allow notifications
- [ ] Set your reminder time and quiet hours
- [ ] Answer your first soil check

## How do I add a plant in MULA?

MULA asks for four things, and only the species is optional.

- **Name**: a nickname, the way you talk about the plant at home, like Momo, Tsubaki or Mame in our sample garden.

- **Species**: the catalog has 20, from Monstera deliciosa and the moth orchid to the snake plant, peace lily, pothos and rosemary. Any other plant can use the “General care plan”.

- **Where it lives**: Indoor, Balcony or Outdoor. Balcony and outdoor plants also get a seasonal temperature check in the cold and hot months.

- **Light**: Low light, Bright, indirect or Direct sun.

(Screenshot: Adding a plant: a nickname, the species, where it lives and how much light it gets.)
Not sure what your plant is? Tap “Not sure what it is?” and take or pick a photo. MULA looks at it with Apple’s on-device image classifier, which recognises plant kinds rather than exact species, so you might see “Looks like: Orchid”. When it is not confident, it says so and you choose the species yourself. The photo never leaves your phone.

Unsure about the light? “Measure”, next to the light choice, opens MULA’s light meter, a Premium feature that estimates light with your iPhone’s camera. The light guide explains what the three light levels mean for houseplants.

Every new plant starts with “A gentle starting plan”: how often to water and feed it in each season. These numbers are starting points, not botanical rules. The free version keeps up to 10 plants.

## How does MULA decide when to water?

It does not decide alone. MULA’s core idea is “A soil check, never an order”. When a plant’s interval is up, MULA asks “How does Momo’s soil feel?” and lets your answer decide:

- **“Dry”** (“Time for a drink”): tap “I watered Momo”. The watering is logged and the next check is planned from today.

- **“A little moist”**: nothing is logged, and MULA asks again in two days.

- **“Wet”**: nothing is logged and this round is skipped.

- **“Not sure”**: MULA shows how to check: “Push a finger 3 cm into the soil. If it comes out clean and dry, it is time to water. If soil sticks to it, wait.”

“Remind me later” postpones the question.

(Screenshot: The soil check: “How does Momo’s soil feel?” A watering is logged only when the answer is dry.)
Why a question instead of a fixed watering day? The University of Maryland Extension says indoor plants should be watered when they need it rather than on a schedule, and the RHS advises checking that a pot needs water before watering. The University of Illinois Extension lists plant type, temperature, humidity and light among the things that change how often a plant needs water. The watering guide goes into more detail.

Feeding is just as gentle. MULA asks “A little nourishment for Momo?” with “Fed today” or “Later”. Fertilizer is optional, and feeding pauses in a plant’s resting season.

## What are the Today, Garden and Settings tabs for?

MULA has three tabs and nothing more. **Today** shows the season, a short status such as “Everyone is cared for.”, and **Upcoming Tasks**: watering, feeding and seasonal checks. If a check is very late, an **Emergency Care** card gives one extra nudge, such as “Momo has waited 7 days for water.” You can change that threshold with “Emergency care after” in Settings; it starts at 7 days.

**Garden** shows every plant as a card with its picture. Tap one to see this season’s plan, its care history as a calendar and its **Journal**: “Little changes are worth keeping.” The free version keeps 5 photos per plant.

(Illustration: Momo’s poster: the photo above, the cut-paper portrait below. Posters come with Premium.)
**Settings** holds your reminders, the seasons and the look of the app: Light Paper or Dark Forest, “Evening calm”, the paper texture, Quiet motion and a soft garden music track of birdsong.

## How do I set the reminder time and quiet hours?

MULA’s reminders are local notifications scheduled by your iPhone, with no server behind them. They keep a simple promise: “Only when a plant needs you. Never at night, never more than once a day for the same plant.” In **Settings** you choose:

- **Remind me at**: the time reminders arrive, 9:00 by default.

- **Quiet hours**: a stretch of the day when MULA sends nothing.

- **Sound**: Kalimba (the default), Wind chime, Water droplet, Singing bowl or the iPhone’s default sound.

You can answer on the notification itself, without opening the app: “Dry · I watered it”, “A little moist” or “Wet” for a soil check, “Fed today” or “Later” for feeding. Tapping it opens that plant. A reminder that groups three or more plants has no buttons. The widgets, Apple Watch and Siri guide covers the other ways to answer.

(Screenshot: Settings: “Remind me at”, “Quiet hours” and the reminder sound.)
> Tip: Pick a reminder time when you are usually at home and near your plants, such as early morning. With the pots right in front of you, a soil check takes a few seconds.
With “Follow the seasons automatically”, reminders shift when the season changes. If you live south of the equator, turn on **Southern hemisphere** in Settings (“Seasons are reversed”). The seasonal care guide explains the four-season plans.

## What is free in MULA and what does Premium add?

MULA is free to download and has no ads, ever. MULA Premium is optional and gives a growing garden more room.

| Free | MULA Premium |

| Up to 10 plants | Unlimited plants and portraits |

| 5 photos per plant | The full photo journal and posters |

| All reminders and soil checks, and viewing the seasonal plans | Editing the seasonal care plan of every plant |

| A seasonal temperature check for balcony and outdoor plants | Weather alerts for frost and heat |

| Small and Lock Screen widgets, the Apple Watch list and Siri | Answer buttons on the medium and large widgets and on Apple Watch |

| No ads and no account, for everyone | Vacation mode and care sheets, and the light meter |

Premium is **Annual**, with a 1-week free trial, renewing yearly until you cancel it in your Apple ID subscriptions, or **Lifetime**: “Pay once. Yours forever.” Prices are shown in the App Store for your country. Purchases are handled by Apple, and “Restore purchases” is in Settings.

## What should I do after setting up MULA?

Let the first week run. Answer each soil check honestly, even when the answer is “Wet”: a skipped round is care too. Add a photo now and then, and the Journal will slowly show each plant changing with the seasons.

If a plant looks unwell, remember that MULA’s plans are starting points and the app cannot diagnose pests or diseases; a local garden centre can help with anything serious. Questions about the app itself are answered in the FAQ and on the support page.

## Questions

**Is MULA free?**
Yes. MULA is free to download and has no ads. The free version keeps up to 10 plants and 5 photos per plant, with all reminders, soil checks, seasonal plans to view, the temperature check, small and Lock Screen widgets, the Apple Watch list and Siri. MULA Premium, Annual with a 1-week free trial or Lifetime, adds unlimited plants and extras such as plan editing, Vacation mode, the light meter and weather alerts.

**Do I need an account to use MULA?**
No. MULA has no account and no server of its own. Your plants, care history, photos and settings are stored on your iPhone, shared with MULA’s own widgets and Apple Watch app, and backed up and synced through your own iCloud.

**What if my plant is not in MULA’s list?**
Add it with the “General care plan”. MULA’s catalog has 20 species, and any other plant can be added this way. You can also try “Not sure what it is?”, which suggests a plant kind from a photo, entirely on your iPhone.

**What happens when I answer “A little moist”?**
Nothing is logged and MULA asks again in two days. A watering is only recorded when you say the soil was dry, so the plan follows what the soil tells you rather than the calendar.

# How often should you water houseplants? When the soil says so
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/how-often-to-water-houseplants/
Language: en

**Short answer:** There is no single right number of days. Water a houseplant when the top 2–5 cm of potting mix feels dry and the pot feels light, then water thoroughly until it drains and empty the saucer. How long that takes depends on the plant, the pot, the light and the season, which is why watering on a fixed day so often leads to overwatering.

- Water when the top 2–5 cm of mix is dry, not when the calendar says so.
- Lift the pot: a dry pot feels clearly lighter than a freshly watered one.
- Pot type, light, warmth, season and plant type all change the rhythm.
- Water thoroughly, let it drain, and never leave the pot standing in water.
- MULA asks how the soil feels and only logs a watering when you say it was dry.

## How often should you water houseplants?

Water a houseplant when its soil is dry a little way down, not when the calendar says it is time. For most leafy houseplants that means the top 2–5 cm of potting mix feels dry and the pot feels noticeably lighter. Then water thoroughly, let the extra run out of the drainage hole, and empty the saucer.

How many days that takes differs in every home. The same monstera may want water within days in a warm, bright summer, and far less often in a cool room in winter. University of Illinois Extension notes that fixed schedules usually don’t work, and the RHS advises checking that a pot needs water before you water it.

## How do you know when a plant needs water?

Your hands are the most reliable tool. Three quick checks cover almost every pot:

- **The finger test.** Push a finger into the mix, a little away from the stem. Extension guides suggest feeling about 2.5 cm (UConn) to 5 cm (University of Illinois) down, roughly to your first or second knuckle. If it feels dry at that depth, it is usually time to water. If it feels cool and damp, or soil clings to your finger, wait.

- **The weight of the pot.** Dry pots feel lighter than wet ones, as the RHS points out. Lift the pot right after a thorough watering to learn its “full” weight; a few days later the difference is easy to feel.

- **A stick for deep pots.** In large containers, push a wooden skewer or dowel to the bottom and pull it out. University of Maryland Extension notes that moist soil will cling to it or darken it.

Leaves alone can mislead you. A wilting plant is often thirsty, but University of Illinois Extension points out that wilting can also be a symptom of overwatering, when damaged roots can no longer take up water. Touch the soil before you reach for the watering can. The guide to overwatering and underwatering signs shows how to tell the two apart.

## Why watering on a fixed day leads to overwatering

A fixed day assumes the plant used the same amount of water every week. It rarely does. Growth slows in the darker months, a cloudy week uses less than a sunny one, and a pot moved away from the window dries more slowly. When you water on schedule anyway, the mix never gets the chance to dry and the roots sit in wet soil.

Roots need air as well as water. The RHS explains that when a pot stays waterlogged, water fills the air spaces in the compost and the roots can drown. Checking first takes a few seconds, and it protects the part of the plant you cannot see.

## What changes how fast the soil dries?

Four things set the rhythm, and all of them shift through the year:

- **The pot.** Unglazed clay is porous and dries faster than plastic or glazed pots (University of Illinois, UConn). A plant that has outgrown a small pot also needs water more often. Every pot should have a drainage hole so extra water can escape (RHS).

- **Light and warmth.** More light and a warmer room usually mean faster water use (UConn). A bright window and a dim hallway are two different climates; the light guide helps you read your spots.

- **The season.** Most houseplants grow actively in spring and summer and dry out faster then. In a cool room in winter, the RHS notes that many can go a week or two without water. Central heating is the exception: a pot near a radiator can dry quickly even in January.

- **The plant itself.** Plants with thick or waxy leaves, or with few leaves, usually need less water (UConn). Succulents hold water in their fleshy leaves and stems, so they ask for much less.

## How often to water monstera, succulents, orchids and ferns

Here are typical patterns by plant group. Treat them as tendencies, not timetables: your soil check still has the final word.

| Plant group | Usual tendency | What to watch |

| Succulents and cacti | Water thoroughly once the surface feels dry in spring and summer; little or no water during the winter rest, roughly November to early March in the northern hemisphere (RHS). | Gritty, free-draining mix and no standing water. Too much water can lead to rot. |

| Tropical foliage (monstera, pothos) | Water while it is growing, letting the top of the soil dry between waterings; keep just moist in winter (RHS, NYBG). | The finger test at 2–5 cm. Yellowing lower leaves can mean too much water. |

| Moth orchids (Phalaenopsis) | In bark, often about once a week in the growing season and a little less in winter; in moss, when the top feels dry (RHS, Clemson Extension). | Pot weight. Keep water out of the crown and let the pot drain fully. |

| Ferns (e.g. Boston fern) | Moist but well-drained compost: water moderately while growing and sparingly in winter (RHS). | Check often; small pots in warm rooms dry fastest. |

A grower’s label may differ for a particular variety, so read yours too.

## Is there an app that reminds you to water plants by checking the soil?

MULA is a calm iPhone app built around exactly this idea: it never orders a watering. When a plant’s interval is up, it asks **“How does Momo’s soil feel?”** and lets your answer decide.

(Screenshot: The soil check in MULA: “How does Momo’s soil feel?”)

- **“Dry”** (“Time for a drink”): tap **“I watered Momo”** and the watering is logged. The next check is planned from today.

- **“A little moist”** (“Check again in 2 days”): nothing is logged, and MULA asks again in two days.

- **“Wet”** (“Skip this round”): nothing is logged and this round is skipped; the next check comes after a full interval.

- **“Not sure”** (“Show me how to check”): MULA explains the finger test. **“Remind me later”** simply postpones the question.

A watering is only recorded when you say the soil was dry. The same rule applies on **Today**, in notifications, in widgets, on Apple Watch and with Siri. The notification buttons “Dry · I watered it”, “A little moist” and “Wet” work without opening the app. So the interval is only the moment MULA asks; the soil decides the rest.

Reminders come only when a plant needs you, never at night and never more than once a day for the same plant. Each plant also has a four-season plan, and with “Follow the seasons automatically” on, the checks shift as the seasons change. The built-in numbers are gentle starting points, not botanical rules. Viewing them is free; editing them is part of MULA Premium. More in the seasonal care guide.

> Tip: Not sure what “dry” feels like? Tap **“Not sure”** on the soil check. MULA shows one simple method: “Push a finger 3 cm into the soil. If it comes out clean and dry, it is time to water. If soil sticks to it, wait.”

(Illustration: Nori, the rubber plant (Ficus elastica) in MULA’s sample garden.)

## A simple watering routine you can keep

- [ ] Push a finger 2–5 cm into the mix, away from the stem
- [ ] Lift the pot and compare it with its watered weight
- [ ] Water only if the mix is dry at that depth
- [ ] Water slowly until it runs from the drainage hole
- [ ] Empty the saucer within an hour or so
- [ ] Use room-temperature water, especially in winter
- [ ] Expect the rhythm to change with season, light and pot

MULA is free to download and keeps up to 10 plants with every reminder and soil check, with no ads and no account. New to it? The quick-start guide walks you through adding your first plant.

## Questions

**How often should I water my monstera?**
When the top few centimetres of potting mix feel dry, rather than on a fixed day. The RHS suggests watering monstera while it is growing and keeping it just moist in winter, so expect to water noticeably less often in the cooler, darker months. Always let the extra water drain away.

**How do I know when to water my plants?**
Push a finger about 2–5 cm into the potting mix. If it feels dry at that depth and the pot feels light, water thoroughly until water runs from the drainage hole. If it feels moist or soil sticks to your finger, check again in a day or two.

**Is there an app that reminds me to water plants?**
MULA, a calm iPhone app, sends a gentle reminder when a plant’s interval is up, but it asks how the soil feels instead of telling you to water. Only “Dry” logs a watering; “A little moist” asks again in two days and “Wet” skips the round. It is free for up to 10 plants, with no ads and no account.

**Should I water houseplants less in winter?**
Usually, yes. Most houseplants grow more slowly in winter and their soil stays moist for longer, especially in a cool room. Heated rooms can still dry pots quickly, so keep checking the soil rather than switching to a new fixed schedule.

# Overwatering vs underwatering: how to tell the signs apart and help your plant
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/overwatering-vs-underwatering-signs/
Language: en

**Short answer:** Check the soil first. An overwatered plant usually sits in soggy soil, with yellowing lower leaves and wilting that does not improve after watering; its roots may be brown, soft and smell bad. An underwatered plant has dry, light soil that may pull away from the pot, crisp brown leaf edges, and drooping that recovers soon after a thorough watering.

- Wilting can mean too much or too little water, so touch the soil before you act.
- Overwatering: soggy soil, yellow lower leaves, soft dark roots, fungus gnats.
- Underwatering: a light pot, crispy brown edges, soil shrinking from the pot.
- To rescue an overwatered plant, stop watering, check drainage and roots, and repot in fresh mix.
- MULA cannot diagnose diseases, but its soil check helps prevent overwatering.

## How can you tell if a plant is overwatered or underwatered?

Touch the soil. An overwatered plant looks unwell while its potting mix is still wet: lower leaves turn yellow, stems may soften, and it can wilt even though the pot is heavy. An underwatered plant looks unwell in dry, light soil: leaf edges turn crisp and brown, and it droops, but usually perks up within hours of a good drink.

The confusing part is that both can make a plant wilt. When roots sit in wet soil for too long, they run short of oxygen, start to die and can no longer take up water, so the plant droops as if it were thirsty (University of Maryland Extension, Clemson Extension). Watering it again only makes things worse. That is why the soil, not the leaves, is the first thing to check.

## Signs of overwatering

- **Yellowing lower leaves.** Wilting or yellowing of the lower and inner leaves is often the first sign of too much moisture (University of Maryland Extension). Clemson Extension notes that yellow leaves are most often a sign of overwatering.

- **Soil that stays soggy.** The mix is still wet days after watering, the pot feels heavy, or water stands in the saucer or decorative outer pot.

- **Wilting in wet soil.** The RHS notes that a plant wilting in wet compost can point to root damage from overwatering, or to root disease.

- **Soft, dark roots with a bad smell.** Healthy roots are usually firm and white. Rotting roots are soft, brown to black, and often smell unpleasant (Chicago Botanic Garden, Iowa State University Extension).

- **Fungus gnats.** Tiny dark flies running over the soil often breed in mix that stays wet. Iowa State University Extension says overwatered houseplants are their most common home, and that letting the soil dry between waterings helps.

- **Dropping leaves.** Either too much or too little water can cause leaf drop (Clemson Extension), so read it together with the soil.

## Signs of underwatering

- **Crispy, brown leaf edges.** The RHS lists brown leaf edges as a possible sign of underwatering. Hot, dry air and salt build-up can brown leaf tips too (Clemson Extension), so check the soil before deciding.

- **Drooping that recovers after watering.** A thirsty plant in dry soil often droops, then lifts again within hours of a thorough watering. If it stays limp in wet soil, think about the roots instead.

- **Soil pulling away from the pot.** Very dry mix shrinks from the sides, and water runs straight down the gap into the saucer without soaking in (UConn Extension).

- **A light pot.** The pot feels much lighter than after watering, and the finger test finds no moisture a few centimetres down.

- **Curling leaves and dropped buds.** Ongoing dryness can bring leaf curling (Clemson Extension) and flower buds that fall before they open (RHS).

For a pot that has dried out completely, UConn Extension suggests setting it in a sink or bucket of water until air bubbles stop rising, then letting it drain well.

## Overwatering vs underwatering: the signs side by side

| What you notice | Overwatered | Underwatered |

| Soil | Wet or soggy for days; heavy pot | Dry a few centimetres down; light pot |

| Leaves | Lower leaves yellow and limp | Edges and tips crisp and brown |

| Wilting | Wilts in wet soil; watering does not help | Droops in dry soil; recovers after watering |

| Roots | Brown to black, soft, may smell bad | Root ball dry and light all the way through |

| Around the pot | Fungus gnats; water standing in the saucer | Soil shrinks from the pot; water runs straight through |

## How to save an overwatered plant

Many overwatered plants recover if you act early. Go gently, one step at a time:

- **Stop watering.** Let the top of the mix dry before you water again, and pour away any water in the saucer or outer pot.

- **Check the drainage.** Every pot should have a drainage hole (RHS). Make sure it is not blocked, and lift the plant out of any decorative pot that holds water.

- **Look at the roots.** If the plant still wilts in wet soil after a few days, ease it out of the pot. Firm, pale roots are a good sign; soft, dark, smelly ones are rotting.

- **Trim what has rotted.** With clean scissors, cut away soft, dark roots, along with yellow or dead leaves (Chicago Botanic Garden, Clemson Extension).

- **Repot in fresh mix.** Use fresh, well-draining potting mix in a clean pot with a drainage hole, rather than the old wet soil. A pot that just fits the remaining roots usually dries more evenly than a much bigger one.

- **Resume normal care.** From now on, check the soil before every watering. New leaves are the sign the plant has settled.

If most of the roots have rotted, recovery is less likely. Chicago Botanic Garden suggests that when more than half the roots are damaged, you might consider starting again.

## When yellow leaves are not about water

Yellowing and drooping have other causes too: too little light, cold draughts, pests, disease, or simply an old leaf being let go. If the soil feels right and the plant keeps declining, or you see spots, webbing, sticky residue or insects, take a clear photo and ask a local nursery, garden centre or your regional extension service. They can look at the plant and know the problems common where you live.

MULA cannot diagnose pests or diseases, and its care plans are starting points, not professional horticultural advice. What it can help with is the most common cause of all: watering on autopilot.

## How a soil-first routine prevents overwatering

Most overwatering is not one big mistake. It is a habit of watering on a set day whether or not the plant used the water. A soil-first routine breaks that habit: check before every watering, water thoroughly only when the mix is dry, and let the season set the pace. The guide on how often to water houseplants goes into the details.

MULA, a calm iPhone app, is built around this idea. When a plant’s interval is up, it asks **“How does Momo’s soil feel?”** instead of telling you to water. Only **“Dry”** logs a watering. **“A little moist”** asks again in two days and **“Wet”** skips the round, so a soggy pot never gets an extra drink just because a date came round.

(Screenshot: Momo’s plant page in MULA: where it lives, its light and this season’s plan.)

Each plant page shows where the plant lives (Indoor, Balcony or Outdoor), its light, and this season’s plan. When a season is set to **Resting**, the plan reads “Less water and no feeding while it rests.” The care history calendar and the photo journal help you notice slow changes, like leaves yellowing over a few weeks. If a spot is too dark, the light guide can help, and seasonal care explains the yearly rhythm.

> Tip: Answered **“Wet”** two rounds in a row? That is a quiet hint the plant is drinking more slowly than its plan expects, perhaps because of less light or a cooler room. Look at its spot first. With MULA Premium you can also lengthen that season’s watering interval.

(Illustration: Mame, the Chinese money plant (Pilea peperomioides) in MULA’s sample garden.)

- [ ] Touch the soil before every watering
- [ ] Water only when the top few centimetres are dry
- [ ] Use pots with drainage holes
- [ ] Empty saucers and outer pots after watering
- [ ] Water less in a plant’s slow season
- [ ] Check the roots if a plant wilts in wet soil
- [ ] Ask a local nursery or extension service about spots, pests or disease

MULA is free to download for up to 10 plants, with every reminder and soil check, no ads and no account.

## Questions

**Can an overwatered plant recover?**
Often, yes, if you act early. Stop watering, let the top of the mix dry, make sure the pot drains and check the roots. Trim soft, dark roots and repot in fresh, well-draining mix. If more than half of the roots are damaged, recovery is less likely.

**Why are the lower leaves on my plant turning yellow?**
Too much water is a common cause, especially when the soil stays wet for days. Old leaves also yellow naturally, and low light, cold or pests can play a part. Check the soil first; if it is soggy, let it dry and look at the drainage.

**Do fungus gnats mean I am overwatering?**
Very often. Fungus gnats breed in potting mix that stays moist, and overwatered houseplants are their most common home indoors. Letting the soil dry between waterings, or repotting in fresh mix, usually reduces them.

**Can MULA tell me what is wrong with my plant?**
No. MULA cannot diagnose pests or diseases, and its plans are starting points, not professional advice. It helps prevent overwatering by asking how the soil feels before a watering is logged. For spots, pests or a plant that keeps declining, ask a local nursery or extension service.

- Clemson Cooperative Extension, HGIC (2025). Houseplant diseases & disorders. https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/houseplant-diseases-disorders/
- Chicago Botanic Garden (n.d.). Overwatered houseplants. https://www.chicagobotanic.org/plant-information/overwatered-houseplants
- Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (2014). Root rots of houseplants. https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/article/2014/02-14/rootrot.html

# How should houseplant care change with the seasons?
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/seasonal-houseplant-care-calendar/
Language: en

**Short answer:** Most houseplants grow when days are long and bright and slow down when they are short and dark, so care follows the light: in spring and summer, water more often, feed regularly and repot if needed; in autumn and winter, water less, feed little or not at all, and keep plants away from cold glass and radiators. Some plants, such as camellias, poinsettias and many orchids, keep their own calendar. MULA gives every plant a four-season plan, and with “Follow the seasons automatically” on, its reminders shift when the season changes.

- Most houseplants grow with long, bright days and slow down in short, dark ones; watering and feeding should follow.
- Spring is the usual time to start feeding again and to repot, once new growth appears.
- In winter, most houseplants need less water and little or no fertilizer; check the soil before you water.
- Camellias, poinsettias and many orchids keep their own calendar, so shape their plan around the plant.
- In MULA, every plant has a four-season plan; a Resting season pauses feeding, and the Southern hemisphere switch reverses the seasons.

## How does houseplant care change through the year?

Most houseplants follow the light. In long, bright days they grow, drink more and can use fertilizer; in short, dark days they slow down and need less water and little or no feeding. The RHS puts the main growing season for houseplants at roughly March to October in the UK.

That gives a simple rhythm to adapt to your home and to each plant:

| Season | Water | Feeding | Watch for |

| Spring | A little more as growth returns | Restart once new growth shows | The usual time to repot |

| Summer | Most often; pots dry faster | Regularly, as the label says | Strong sun through glass, heat |

| Autumn | Gradually less | Ease off; stop for many plants | Bringing outdoor plants back in |

| Winter | Least; check the soil first | Little or none | Cold glass, radiators, dry air |

Treat it as a starting point, not a rule: the soil is always a better guide than the calendar. The guide to how often to water houseplants explains how to read it.

## Spring: when to repot houseplants and start feeding again

As the days lengthen, new leaves usually appear. That is the signal to wake the routine gently: water a little more often as the plant uses more, and start feeding again once growth has clearly resumed. Iowa State University Extension recommends fertilizing regularly in spring and summer, while plants are actively growing. Follow the dose on the label.

Spring is also the classic time to repot. Penn State Extension says the best time is spring, when a plant naturally begins its seasonal growth, and the RHS adds that plants potted on in spring can establish during the growing season. Most don’t need it every year: the RHS suggests potting on every two to three years. Signs it is time, according to Penn State, include roots growing through the drainage holes or circling the root ball. Choose a pot only slightly larger than the old one.

## Summer: more water, more light, and heat to watch for

The RHS notes that with higher temperatures plants are more active and dry out faster, so the gaps between waterings usually shrink. Keep checking the soil first, though.

The RHS also warns that strong summer sun can scorch susceptible plants through glass, and that excessive heat makes plants that prefer cooler conditions dehydrate and wilt. If your plants spend the summer on a balcony, see the guide to protecting balcony plants from frost and heat.

## Autumn: slowing down and bringing plants back inside

As the days shorten, growth slows, and care can slow with it: water a little less often and ease off feeding. Iowa State Extension advises stopping fertilizer in autumn and winter for plants that are no longer actively growing.

Houseplants that spent the summer outdoors should come in before the cold, not after it. Iowa State suggests bringing them inside when nights dip consistently to around 10°C (50°F), since many are damaged once nights fall to about 7°C. Check them for pests before they come in, and expect a few dropped leaves while they adjust.

## Should I fertilize houseplants in winter?

For most houseplants, little or not at all. Iowa State Extension says fertilizer is generally not necessary in winter because most houseplants are not growing. Clemson’s Home & Garden Information Center notes that many indoor plants with little or no artificial light enter a resting stage in the short days and should not be fed while they rest. The RHS is slightly softer: feed no more than once a month, because light levels are too low. Plants under artificial light, and those in the next section, can be exceptions.

Winter watering is mostly patience. With less light and lower temperatures, plants grow less and need less water, says the RHS; in a cool room many can go a week or two without. Central heating dries the air, though, and pots can dry out faster in a warm room. So water by the soil, not by the date. If leaves yellow or the compost stays wet for days, the guide to signs of overwatering can help.

Mind the spot, too. The RHS says houseplants benefit from full sunlight when winter daylight is weak; the light guide helps you choose a window. It also warns that the space behind drawn curtains can get very cold, that cold draughts can shock a plant, and that radiators can brown leaf edges. Grouping plants, or standing them on a tray of moist gravel, raises the humidity around them.

## Plants that keep their own calendar

Spring growth and winter rest is a useful default, but some popular plants don’t follow it.

- **Camellia.** The RHS says Camellia japonica flowers in late winter and early spring, and its flowers are formed over summer, so the soil shouldn’t dry out then. It also advises not feeding after the end of July, as late feeding can cause bud drop.

- **Poinsettia.** Its season is winter. Purdue Extension calls it a long-night plant: to bloom again, it needs complete darkness every night from early October to mid-December.

- **Moth orchids (Phalaenopsis).** They can flower at any time of year, says the RHS. In winter it suggests bright light, slightly less water and little or no feed. A spot about 5°C cooler for a month or so can encourage a flower spike, but buds drop if the plant gets too cold.

## How MULA’s four-season plans work

In MULA, every plant has a four-season plan: for spring, summer, autumn and winter, it sets how often to water and to feed, with a short tip for the season. A season can be marked **Resting**: “Less water and no feeding while it rests.” Feeding reminders pause then and start again on the first day of the next season that has feeding. Each plan also holds a temperature range, such as “Happy between 15 and 30°C”.

(Screenshot: Seasonal care: water and feed every N days for each season, the temperature range and “Follow the seasons automatically”.)

With **“Follow the seasons automatically”** on, reminders shift when the season changes. South of the equator, the **Southern hemisphere** switch in Settings reverses the seasons. **Today** shows the season above the headline, for example “Today · Autumn”.

The interval is never an order. When it is up, MULA asks “How does Momo’s soil feel?” and logs a watering only when you answer “Dry · I watered it”. “A little moist” asks again in two days, and “Wet” skips the round. In a cool winter room, that question matters more than any number.

New plants start with “A gentle starting plan”, and the built-in plans are starting points, not botanical rules. Viewing every plan is free; editing the season numbers is part of MULA Premium.

> Tip: Before you change a number, let the soil check speak for a season. If you keep answering **“A little moist”** in winter, the plant’s winter interval could be longer.

(Illustration: Ajisai, the bigleaf hydrangea from MULA’s sample garden.)

## A seasonal houseplant checklist

- [ ] Spring: feed again once new growth shows
- [ ] Spring: repot if roots grow through the drainage holes
- [ ] Autumn: bring outdoor houseplants in before nights reach about 10°C
- [ ] Winter: water only when the soil is dry
- [ ] Winter: keep plants away from radiators and cold glass
- [ ] All year: turn on “Follow the seasons automatically”

Seasons don’t switch overnight, and neither do plants. Let the calendar remind you, and let the plant have the final word.

## Questions

**Should I fertilize houseplants in winter?**
Usually little or not at all. Most houseplants are not actively growing in winter, so Iowa State University Extension says fertilizer is generally not necessary, and the RHS suggests feeding no more than once a month. Plants under artificial light and winter-flowering plants can be exceptions; follow the label.

**When is the best time to repot houseplants?**
Usually in spring, when a plant begins its seasonal growth, so it can settle in during the growing season. Repot when roots grow through the drainage holes or circle the root ball, into a pot only slightly larger. The RHS suggests potting on every two to three years.

**How often should I water houseplants in winter?**
Less often than in summer, but there is no single number. In a cool room many houseplants can go a week or two without water, while central heating can dry pots out faster. Check the soil before you water rather than following a fixed day.

**Does MULA change my reminders when the season changes?**
Yes. Every plant has a four-season plan, and with “Follow the seasons automatically” on, reminders shift when the season changes. A season marked Resting pauses feeding until the next season that has feeding. The Southern hemisphere switch in Settings reverses the seasons.

**Can I edit MULA’s seasonal plans for free?**
Viewing every plant’s seasonal plan is free. Editing the season numbers is part of MULA Premium, available as Annual with a 1-week free trial or as Lifetime. The built-in plans are starting points you can shape around your own plants.

# How much light does my houseplant need? Low light, bright indirect light and direct sun, explained
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/how-much-light-do-houseplants-need/
Language: en

**Short answer:** Many leafy houseplants do best in bright, indirect light: near a window with a wide view of the sky, but out of strong sun on the leaves. As a rough guide from extension services, low light is under about 1,000 lux (100 foot-candles), bright indirect light about 1,000 to 5,000 lux, high light up to about 10,000 lux and direct sun above that, though sources draw the lines differently. Stretched, leaning growth usually means too little light; pale, scorched patches usually mean too much.

- Many leafy houseplants do best in bright, indirect light; cacti, succulents and citrus want direct sun.
- Rough ranges: low light under about 1,000 lux, bright indirect about 1,000 to 5,000 lux, direct sun above about 10,000 lux.
- Light drops quickly as you move back from a window, and it changes with the season.
- Stretching and leaning point to too little light; pale, scorched patches point to too much.
- A phone reading, including MULA’s Premium light meter, is an estimate: compare spots rather than trust one number.

## How much light does a houseplant need?

Many of the leafy plants we keep indoors do best in bright, indirect light: close enough to a window to see a wide piece of sky, but out of strong sun falling on the leaves for hours. A smaller group, such as cacti, succulents and citrus, wants direct sun. Others, like snake plant, ZZ plant and peace lily, are known for coping with low light.

Light for plants is measured in lux or foot-candles; one foot-candle is about 10.8 lux. Roughly, low light is under about 100 foot-candles (around 1,000 lux), bright indirect light runs to several thousand lux, and direct sun through a window starts around 10,000 lux. Published ranges differ, so treat every number as a neighbourhood, not an address.

## Low light vs bright indirect light vs direct sun

Plant labels use these words loosely. Here is what they usually mean in a room, with the rough midday ranges published by the University of Maryland Extension and UF/IFAS, converted to lux and rounded.

| Light level | Where you usually find it | Foot-candles | Lux (rounded) |

| Low light | Far from windows, or near a north-facing window | 25–100 | about 250–1,000 |

| Medium to bright, indirect | Near an east- or west-facing window, out of direct rays | 100–500 | about 1,000–5,000 |

| High light | Close to a south- or west-facing window, some direct sun | 500–1,000 | about 5,000–10,000 |

| Direct sun | An unshaded south-facing window or a sunroom | over 1,000 | over about 10,000 |

Other services draw the lines elsewhere: Illinois Extension uses benchmarks of about 75, 150, 300 and 1,500 foot-candles for low, medium, high and direct light. Maryland Extension’s lists also hint at which plants sit where: snake plant, ZZ plant and peace lily in low light, rubber plant and dracaena in medium-bright light, cacti, succulents and citrus in direct sun. “Tolerates low light” usually means a plant copes there, not that it grows its best there.

### How many lux does a monstera need?

There is no single official number. NC State Extension describes Monstera deliciosa as liking moderate brightness but not direct sunlight, with variegated plants needing more light than plain green ones. That is the medium to bright indirect band above, roughly 1,000 to 5,000 lux around midday. Kept well below it, a monstera usually grows slowly, with smaller leaves.

## How window direction and distance change the light

In the northern hemisphere, a south-facing window is usually the brightest spot in a home. Nebraska Extension offers a useful comparison: if a south window gives 100%, east and west windows give about 60% and a north window about 20%. West-facing windows also tend to run warmer than east-facing ones. In the southern hemisphere, swap north and south.

Distance matters even more. Light falls off rapidly as you move away from the glass; Nebraska Extension points out that moving a plant only slightly further back cuts the light very quickly. In Illinois Extension’s rough guide, the spot right in front of a north window counts as medium light, but a few feet back it is already low light.

Curtains, insect screens, trees, buildings and the season take light away too. Winter sun is lower and the days are shorter, and Nebraska Extension notes that a plant growing well in an east window in summer may need a south window in winter.

## Signs your plant is not getting enough light

Too little light shows slowly, over weeks:

- **Stretching:** long, thin stems with wide gaps between the leaves, often called leggy growth.

- **Leaning** toward the window, because light reaches the plant from one side.

- **Smaller new leaves** and a paler colour than the older ones.

- **No flowers** on plants that normally bloom.

Moving the plant closer to a window, or to a brighter one, usually helps the next leaves; stretched stems won’t shrink back, but they can often be trimmed in the right season. A plant in low light also uses water more slowly, which is one more reason to touch the soil before watering, as in the guide to how often to water houseplants.

## Signs your plant is getting too much light

Too much direct sun usually shows faster. Nebraska Extension calls it sunburn: pale patches that eventually turn brown and die, often on the side facing the glass. Maryland Extension suggests protecting houseplants from strong direct sun in the summer months.

Scorched patches don’t turn green again, so move the plant back from the window or behind a sheer curtain and judge by the new leaves. When moving a plant into a much brighter spot, doing it in steps over a week or two is usually gentler. And not every brown leaf is about light: soil that stays wet can leave similar marks, so rule that out with the guide to signs of overwatering.

(Illustration: Ran, a moth orchid, as a MULA poster: photo above, cut-paper portrait below.)

## How to measure light for plants with your phone

UF/IFAS suggests a hand-held digital light meter is often the best option. Phone apps are handier, and UF/IFAS says they are usually accurate enough to show a change in light levels but should only be used for approximations. That is the honest way to use any phone reading: to compare spots, not to get a laboratory number.

- Measure where the leaves will be, not on the windowsill.

- Take readings mid-morning, at midday and in the late afternoon.

- Measure again when the seasons change.

## MULA’s light meter: an estimate in lux

MULA’s light meter is part of MULA Premium. Open it from the sun icon in **Garden**, or tap **Measure** next to the light choice when you add a plant. Hold your iPhone where the plant will live, back camera facing the window. MULA reads the camera’s exposure and turns it into an approximate value, such as “About 2,400 lux · an estimate”.

(Screenshot: The light meter: “About 2,400 lux · an estimate”, read as Bright, indirect, with plants that would like the spot.)

The reading is sorted into the three light choices you pick when adding a plant:

- **Low light:** under about 800 lux.

- **Bright, indirect:** about 800 to 10,000 lux.

- **Direct sun:** above about 10,000 lux.

The bands are broad on purpose and roughly in line with the published ranges above; MULA folds medium and high light into one “Bright, indirect” band. Below the reading, “Plants that would like it here” or “Your plants in this spot” show which plants suit that light.

It is an estimate, and MULA says so: a phone camera is not a lab instrument, and light changes with the hour and the season. Take a few readings and trust the pattern more than any single number. No photo is taken or saved, and the reading happens on your iPhone. Choosing a light level by hand when you add a plant is free.

> Tip: Take three readings in the same spot: mid-morning, midday and late afternoon. If the label jumps from “Bright, indirect” to “Direct sun” around noon, that spot gets a few hours of sun, which is worth knowing before you choose a plant for it.

## Light, water and the seasons work together

As the days shorten, many houseplants slow down and need water less often, then pick up again in spring. MULA’s four-season care plans can follow that rhythm, shifting reminders when the season changes; the guide to seasonal plant care explains how. Whatever the season, the soil check still decides whether a plant gets water.

## Questions

**What does bright, indirect light mean?**
It is a spot near a window where the plant sees plenty of sky, but the sun’s rays do not fall on its leaves for long. In extension tables it is roughly 100 to 500 foot-candles, or about 1,000 to 5,000 lux at midday, though sources draw the edges differently.

**How many lux is low light for plants?**
Extension tables such as the University of Maryland’s put low light at about 25 to 100 foot-candles, roughly 250 to 1,000 lux. MULA’s light meter treats readings under about 800 lux as low light. Plants such as snake plant, ZZ plant and peace lily are known for coping with it.

**Can I measure light for plants with my phone?**
Yes, roughly. UF/IFAS says phone apps are usually good enough to show changes in light but should be treated as approximations. MULA’s Premium light meter uses the back camera’s exposure to estimate lux, sorts the spot into low light, bright indirect or direct sun, and does not take or save a photo.

**How much light does a monstera need?**
NC State Extension describes Monstera deliciosa as liking moderate brightness but not direct sunlight, with variegated plants needing more light. In lux that is roughly the 1,000 to 5,000 range at midday: near a bright window, out of strong direct sun.

**Is a north-facing window enough for houseplants?**
In the northern hemisphere, a north window gives about a fifth of the light of a south window, according to Nebraska Extension. Right in front of it is roughly medium light, and a few feet back it drops to low light, so it suits plants that cope with lower light. In the southern hemisphere the same is true of south-facing windows.

## Sources

- University of Maryland Extension (2023). Lighting for Indoor Plants. https://extension.umd.edu/resource/lighting-indoor-plants
- UF/IFAS Extension Gardening Solutions (n.d.). Light for Houseplants. https://gardeningsolutions.ifas.ufl.edu/plants/houseplants/light-for-houseplants/
- Nebraska Extension in Lancaster County (2020). Let There Be Light… for Your Houseplants. https://lancaster.unl.edu/let-there-be-light-your-houseplants
- University of Illinois Extension (n.d.). Houseplants: Lighting. https://extension.illinois.edu/houseplants/lighting
- N.C. Cooperative Extension (n.d.). Monstera deliciosa. Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox. https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/monstera-deliciosa/

# How do you protect balcony plants from frost and heat waves?
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/protect-balcony-plants-from-frost-and-heat/
Language: en

**Short answer:** Potted plants feel frost and heat sooner than plants in the ground, because their roots are more exposed. Before a frosty night, group pots against a sheltered house wall, wrap the pots, cover tender plants with fleece or bring them under cover, and avoid watering; in a heat wave, water early, shade pots from the midday sun, mulch the compost and keep dark or metal pots out of full sun. MULA’s Premium Weather alerts compare the Apple Weather forecast with each balcony or outdoor plant’s temperature range and warn you at 18:00 the evening before a cold night, or at 08:00 on the morning of a hot day.

- Roots in pots are more exposed than roots in the ground, so container plants feel cold and heat sooner.
- Before frost: group pots against a sheltered wall, wrap the pots, fleece or shelter tender plants, and avoid watering.
- In a heat wave: water early, shade pots at midday, mulch, and keep dark or metal pots out of full sun.
- MULA’s free version includes a seasonal temperature check for balcony and outdoor plants in the cold and hot months.
- Premium Weather alerts use the Apple Weather forecast and a location rounded to about 1 km: 18:00 before a cold night, 08:00 on a hot morning.

## Why are balcony plants in pots more at risk from frost and heat?

Because their roots have nowhere to hide. In the ground, roots sit deep in soil that buffers the cold; in a pot, only the compost and the pot wall stand between them and the air. The RHS notes that container plants are more susceptible to cold because their roots are more exposed than those buried deep in the earth, and Iowa State University Extension points out that the roots of most trees and shrubs are far less cold-hardy than their stems. A plant that copes with a frost in a border can be hurt by the same night on a balcony.

Heat works the same way. N.C. Cooperative Extension warns that black or dark containers in the sun can heat up fast, with soil 20 to 30°F (roughly 11 to 17°C) warmer than the surrounding air, and that roots are far more heat-sensitive than leaves. So in both seasons the answer is similar: protect the pot, not only the plant.

## How to protect balcony plants on a frosty night

Act when frost is first forecast: the RHS says protective wrappings should go on at the first sign of frosts.

- **Move pots against the house wall and group them.** The RHS says grouping containers close together near a house wall in winter helps protect roots from the cold. The base of a sunny wall (south-facing in the northern hemisphere) is one of the warmer places.

- **Wrap the pot, not just the plant.** Bubble polythene or straw around the container helps stop the roots freezing, says the RHS.

- **Cover tender plants overnight.** Use horticultural fleece, in a double layer on the coldest nights, or an old sheet. Heavier grades of fleece give about 2°C of protection, according to the RHS, so the most tender plants are safer under cover.

- **Bring the most tender plants in.** Move them under temporary cover for the cold spell: a sheltered spot, a cold greenhouse or a cool conservatory.

- **Raise pots off wet floors.** The RHS suggests standing containers on bricks or pot feet so the drainage holes stay clear.

Even hardy plants appreciate this in a pot. The RHS describes camellias as generally hardy, yet for container-grown ones it still suggests moving the pot nearer the house or into a sheltered corner, wrapping the plant in fleece, or moving it into a cold greenhouse in freezing spells. Camellia japonica flowers in late winter and early spring, and the RHS notes that spring frosts can damage blossom.

(Illustration: Tsubaki, the Japanese camellia from MULA’s sample garden: hardy, yet glad of a sheltered corner when it lives in a pot.)

## Should you water potted plants before a frost?

Generally, no. The RHS advises avoiding watering containers when frost is forecast, and warns that waterlogged compost, especially in winter, can cause roots to rot. Remove saucers and trays before winter so pots don’t stand in water, and if pots stay out all winter, choose frost-proof ones, as terracotta can crack.

That doesn’t mean letting everything dry to dust. The RHS notes that evergreens in containers may need watering during dry spells in winter. If the compost is dry, water on a milder day rather than just before a freezing night.

## How to protect potted plants in a heat wave

The RHS suggests checking pots daily in warm or windy weather and twice a day when it is hot; in summer dry spells you may need to water every day or every other day. Feel the compost first, as the guide to how often to water explains.

- **Water early.** The RHS recommends early morning or early evening, when less water evaporates from the compost. UC Agriculture and Natural Resources (UC ANR) suggests watering deeply in the early morning the day before the heat arrives.

- **Shade the midday sun.** UC ANR advises blocking as much midday sun as possible: move pots into shade or against a shadier wall (north-facing in the northern hemisphere), or use 30 to 50% shade cloth.

- **Mulch the compost.** Mulching pots reduces water lost by evaporation, says the RHS, though careful watering is still needed; UC ANR adds that mulch helps protect roots.

- **Mind dark and metal pots.** Dark containers heat up fast in the sun, thin black plastic nursery pots included, and the RHS notes that metal pots heat up in sunshine, baking the compost. Keep them out of full sun.

- **Group pots and empty saucers.** Grouping pots gives mutual shade and raises local humidity, says the RHS. On hot days, UC ANR suggests emptying saucers after watering, as shallow water heats up quickly, and checking the temperature of hose water before it reaches the roots.

## Late frosts and early chills: the in-between nights

Frost isn’t only a winter problem. The RHS notes that late spring frosts still occur and can scorch or kill tender growth, and advises putting tender plants out only when nights stay consistently above 7°C, after two to three weeks of getting them used to outdoor conditions. In autumn the turn comes the other way: Iowa State Extension suggests bringing houseplants that summered outdoors back inside when nights dip consistently to around 10°C (50°F). For the wider rhythm of the year, see the seasonal houseplant care calendar.

## How MULA watches the temperature for your balcony plants

When you add a plant, MULA asks where it lives: **Indoor**, **Balcony** or **Outdoor**. Each plant also has a temperature range in its seasonal plan, such as “Happy between 15 and 30°C”. In the free version, balcony and outdoor plants get a seasonal temperature check in the cold and hot months.

**Weather alerts** (Premium) go further. Turn them on in **Settings → Reminders → Weather alerts**. MULA then takes the Apple Weather forecast for the next three days and compares its lows and highs with the temperature range of each balcony and outdoor plant.

- **Cold night:** an alert the evening before, at 18:00, so you have the evening to move pots or find the fleece.

- **Hot day:** an alert that morning, at 08:00, in time to water early and set up shade.

- **Quiet hours:** if either time falls inside them, the alert is moved out.

**Today** then shows a line such as “Cold Night Ahead · 2°C tonight”, listing only the plants that are affected.

(Screenshot: Today with a “Cold Night Ahead” line for the balcony plants.)

Your location stays approximate. MULA asks once, rounds it to about 1 km and keeps it on your iPhone; only that rounded point is sent to Apple Weather, and there is no MULA account or server. The Apple Weather mark and a “Data sources” link appear wherever the forecast is shown. Weather alerts also keep working in Vacation Mode, so a cold night at home still reaches you while you are away; see the guide to plant care while you’re on vacation.

> Tip: Choose **Balcony** or **Outdoor** for every plant that lives outside. Weather alerts and the seasonal temperature check only look at those plants, so a balcony pot saved as Indoor won’t be watched.

## A frost and heat checklist for balcony plants

- [ ] Frost forecast: move pots together against the house wall
- [ ] Wrap pots in bubble polythene or straw
- [ ] Fleece tender plants overnight, or bring them under cover
- [ ] Skip watering, stand pots on feet and remove saucers
- [ ] Heat forecast: water deeply early in the morning
- [ ] Shade pots at midday and mulch the compost
- [ ] Move dark and metal pots out of full sun

Most of these steps take minutes; the hard part is remembering them on the right evening.

## Questions

**Should I water my potted plants before a frost?**
Generally no. The RHS advises avoiding watering containers when frost is forecast, because waterlogged compost in winter can rot roots. If evergreens in pots are dry during a winter dry spell, water them on a milder day instead.

**Does horticultural fleece protect plants from frost?**
It helps a little. The RHS says heavier grades of fleece give about 2°C of protection and suggests a double layer on the coldest nights. For pots, also wrap the container and group pots against a sheltered wall; the most tender plants are safer under cover.

**How do I keep potted plants cool in a heat wave?**
Water early in the morning (UC ANR suggests deeply, the day before the heat arrives), shade pots from the midday sun, mulch the compost, group pots together and keep dark or metal pots out of full sun. Check pots daily, and twice a day in hot weather.

**When should I bring balcony houseplants inside in autumn?**
Before the cold arrives. Iowa State University Extension suggests moving houseplants indoors when nights dip consistently to around 10°C (50°F), since many are damaged once nights fall to about 7°C. Check them for pests first.

**How does MULA warn me about frost and heat, and is it free?**
The free version includes a seasonal temperature check for balcony and outdoor plants in the cold and hot months. Weather alerts are Premium: MULA compares the Apple Weather forecast for the next three days with each balcony or outdoor plant’s temperature range and alerts you at 18:00 before a cold night or at 08:00 on a hot morning, using a location rounded to about 1 km.

- RHS (n.d.). Frost damage. https://www.rhs.org.uk/prevention-protection/frost-damage

# How to keep your houseplants alive while you’re on vacation
URL: https://guledaaydemir.github.io/MULA/guides/keep-plants-alive-on-vacation/
Language: en

**Short answer:** For a weekend, most houseplants need nothing more than a soil check and a thorough watering for the ones that are dry. For one to two weeks, also move plants back from hot, sunny windows, group them and give the thirstiest a water reserve, such as a wick or capillary matting. For longer trips, the most reliable plan is a neighbour or friend who checks the soil and waters only what is dry.

- Most houseplants manage a few days alone; the RHS says trips of more than a week call for some planning.
- Before you leave, touch the soil and water thoroughly only the plants that are dry.
- Move plants out of hot sun, group them, and keep the house no warmer than usual.
- Wicks, capillary matting and clear covers give a small water reserve; test them before you go.
- MULA’s Vacation Mode (Premium) can pause or keep reminders and share a plain-text care sheet with a helper.

## How do you keep houseplants alive while you’re on vacation?

Match the plan to the length of the trip. Most houseplants manage a few days on their own if they start with moist soil and stay out of hot sun. For a week or two, they usually need a little help: a cooler spot, company from other plants and a small reserve of water. For anything longer, the gentlest plan is still a person who comes in, touches the soil and waters what is dry. The aim is steady, moderate moisture, not soil left soggy for days, which can harm roots too.

## How long can houseplants go without water?

It depends on the plant, the pot, the season and your home. The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) says most houseplants tolerate a few days’ absence, that trips of more than a week call for some creative measures, and that in winter many can be left for a week or two if the room doesn’t get too cold for them. The University of Saskatchewan notes that small pots and clay pots dry out faster, and that cacti and succulents tolerate drought far better than leafy plants.

### A weekend away

Check each plant’s soil the day before you leave. Water the dry ones thoroughly, let them drain, and leave the rest as they are. In hot weather, pull plants back from sunny windows. That is usually all.

### One to two weeks

Do the same soil check, then move plants somewhere cooler, group them, and give the thirstiest a water reserve using one of the methods below. In winter, the RHS suggests moving plants away from cold windows and watering so the compost is moist but not waterlogged.

### Three weeks or longer

Self-watering tricks rarely stretch this far. For trips longer than a couple of weeks, the RHS suggests asking a trusted neighbour, friend or relative to water. Even an occasional visit can make a real difference.

(Illustration: Tsubaki, a Japanese camellia, as a MULA poster: photo above, cut-paper portrait below.)

## What to do before you leave

- **Touch the soil first.** Water thoroughly only where the top of the soil is dry, and let the pot drain. A plant that is still moist needs nothing extra.

- **Move plants out of hot sun.** The RHS and the University of Saskatchewan both suggest a cooler room or a spot away from bright windows, which slows drying.

- **Group them.** The University of Missouri suggests grouping plants with easy access to water, which also makes a helper’s job quicker.

- **Keep the house no warmer than usual.** The same article advises against raising the thermostat while you are away, since warmth dries pots faster.

- **Leave cacti and succulents be.** The RHS treats them as the exception: they usually don’t need watering during a holiday.

## Self-watering tricks: wicks, capillary matting and covers

These give plants a slow, steady supply of water. Set them up a few days early; the University of Saskatchewan suggests testing a method before you leave to see what works for your plants.

- **A wick.** Run a cotton string or a strip of capillary matting from a large container of water into the pot’s soil; capillary action carries the water across. NC Cooperative Extension suggests keeping the reservoir a little higher than the pot, and the RHS recommends this for large single pots.

- **Capillary matting for groups.** Lay the matting on the draining board with one end in a sink of water, then press the pots onto the wet mat. The RHS suggests watering clay pots first, and notes that pots with broken crocks in the base may not draw well.

- **A clear cover.** For short absences, the RHS suggests a clear lid, a propagator or a reused clear plastic bag held off the leaves with canes. Keep covered plants out of direct sun.

- **Watering spikes.** A spike on a water bottle, pushed into the soil, lets water seep out slowly; the University of Missouri notes bottles work for a short time.

- **Self-watering pots.** The RHS sees these reservoir pots as a long-term way of growing rather than a holiday fix, so it isn’t worth repotting just for a trip.

> Tip: Do a trial run the weekend before you go. Set up the wick or mat, leave it for three or four days, then touch the soil. You will know whether it gives too little, too much or just enough.

## Asking a plant sitter: what to tell them

For longer trips, a neighbour or friend who comes in is still the most dependable plan. Make their visits easy:

- Walk them round the plants before you go; the University of Missouri suggests going over each plant’s watering needs together.

- Group the plants near a sink or tap, and water the dry ones deeply before you lock the door.

- Ask them to touch the soil and water only what is dry, rather than watering everything on every visit.

- Leave a short note, plant by plant.

The third point matters most: a helper who waters every pot each time can overwater the plants that were fine. Soil first, then water, as the guide to how often to water houseplants explains.

## Vacation Mode in MULA

In MULA, **Vacation Mode** in **Settings** is made for this; it is part of MULA Premium. The screen asks “Going away?”. You pick your **Leaving** and **Back home** dates and one of three options:

- **Pause reminders:** “Nothing is marked as done. You review on return.”

- **Someone is helping:** “Share a care sheet with names and notes.” Add a name under “Who is helping?”, then tap “Share the care sheet” to send your helper a plain-text care sheet, plant by plant.

- **Keep reminders:** “I’ll check from afar.”

If plants are already due, MULA says so, for example “3 plants are due a soil check before you leave.” Tap **Start away mode**, and **Today** shows a quiet line such as “Away mode · back 24 Nov”.

(Screenshot: Vacation Mode: your dates, “Who is helping?” and “Share the care sheet”.)

Vacation Mode never marks a task as done: MULA can’t know whether a plant was watered, so it doesn’t pretend. Weather alerts (also Premium) keep working while you’re away, so a frost or heat warning for balcony and outdoor plants still reaches you to pass on to your helper. See frost and heat on the balcony.

## Coming home: how to check your plants after a trip

Unless you chose **Keep reminders**, MULA greets you on your return with “Welcome home to your garden. Nothing was marked as done for you. Let’s see how everyone is.” Then reminders resume.

Go round slowly. Touch each plant’s soil and give it what it needs: water, food or nothing at all. There is no need to water everything at once; a plant your helper watered yesterday doesn’t need more today. If leaves are limp while the soil is wet, the guide to signs of overwatering can help.

## Pre-trip plant checklist

Tick these off in the days before you go.

- [ ] Touch the soil of every plant
- [ ] Water thoroughly only the plants that are dry
- [ ] Move plants back from hot windows, and from cold glass in winter
- [ ] Group plants together, near water if someone is helping
- [ ] Test wicks or capillary matting a few days early
- [ ] Leave cacti and succulents as they are
- [ ] Keep the house no warmer than usual
- [ ] Walk your helper round the plants and leave a note
- [ ] Set your dates in MULA’s Vacation Mode

## Questions

**How long can houseplants go without water?**
It depends on the plant, the pot and the season. The RHS says most houseplants tolerate a few days’ absence, trips of more than a week need some planning, and in winter many can manage a week or two if the room doesn’t get too cold. Cacti and succulents can usually go much longer than leafy plants.

**Should I water my plants right before going on vacation?**
Water the ones whose soil is dry, thoroughly, and let them drain. Plants that are still moist don’t need extra, because soil that stays soggy for days can harm roots. Cacti and succulents can usually be left as they are.

**Do self-watering wicks really work?**
They can help for a week or two. A cotton string or a strip of capillary matting carries water from a container into the soil by capillary action. Test the setup a few days before you leave, and for longer trips ask someone to check the plants.

**Does MULA mark plants as watered while I’m away?**
No. Vacation Mode never marks a task as done, because MULA can’t know what was watered while you were gone. When you’re back, reminders resume and you check each plant’s soil yourself. Vacation Mode is part of MULA Premium.

## Sources

- Royal Horticultural Society (n.d.). Houseplants: holiday care. https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/types/houseplants/holiday-care
- University of Saskatchewan, Gardening at USask (2018). Watering houseplants & containers while on vacation. https://gardening.usask.ca/articles-and-lists/articles-indoor-growing/watering-houseplants-while-on-vacation.php
- University of Missouri Integrated Pest Management (2023). Summer Vacation Planning Includes Plant Care. https://ipm.missouri.edu/MEG/2023/7/vacationPlantCare-MW
- N.C. Cooperative Extension, Pender County Center (2022). How to Save Your Houseplants While Vacationing. https://pender.ces.ncsu.edu/2022/02/how-to-save-your-houseplants-while-vacationing
